title: Foundations for Christian Technology
description: A Christian companion to the Center for Humane Technology's Foundations of Humane Technology: fifteen modules in five movements, walking the shape of the gospel story from lament to commissioning.
purpose: Upgrade the collective wisdom of the church to improve awareness and decision-making in a world facing emergent 'godlike' technology
thumbnailAlt: Foundations for Christian Technology course cover

contributorPresences.name: Matthew Dowell
contributorPresences.contribution: Author and steward of Foundations for Christian Technology. Adapted the Center for Humane Technology curriculum with biblical foundations and Christian theological integration.

contributorPresences.name: Tristan Harris
contributorPresences.contribution: Co-founder of the Center for Humane Technology. His work exposing the attention economy and advocating for humane technology provides the foundational structure and vision for this course.

contributorPresences.name: Aza Raskin
contributorPresences.contribution: Co-founder of the Center for Humane Technology. His systems thinking approach to technology ethics and work on AI safety deeply influenced the course's analytical framework.

contributorPresences.name: Randima (Randy) Fernando
contributorPresences.contribution: Executive Director of the Center for Humane Technology. His leadership in developing the Foundations of Humane Technology course provided the pedagogical structure adapted in this Christian edition.

contributorPresences.name: Daniel Schmachtenberger
contributorPresences.contribution: His work on the metacrisis, existential risk, and civilizational design directly inspired the 'A Problem Well Stated' module. His articulation of generator functions and systemic risk informs the course's analysis of technology's role in civilizational challenges.

chapters.title: Movement I: Waking Up — Lament & Sight
chapters.description: Lament & sight: from assuming the church stands outside the crisis to seeing it clearly.

modules.title: 1. The Church Dilemma
modules.description: from assuming the church stands outside the crisis → to honest lament that we are inside the attention economy.

steps.stepNarrative: from assuming the church stands outside the crisis → to honest lament that we are inside the attention economy.
learningObjectives: Describe the attention economy's business model and the Ledger of Harms as portrayed in *The Social Dilemma*.
Identify where the race for attention already touches their own weekly habits and their congregation's life.
Contrast what Scripture binds to our hands and foreheads (Deuteronomy 6) with what our devices bind there now.
Practice biblical lament as the church's first faithful response to systemic harm — refusing both denial and despair.
Commit to the class covenant that will govern how this cohort learns together.

modules.title: 2. Systems Thinking
modules.description: from blaming individuals → to seeing interconnected systems as the arena of stewardship and the Body of Christ.

steps.stepNarrative: from blaming individuals → to seeing interconnected systems as the arena of stewardship and the Body of Christ.
learningObjectives: Distinguish complicated from complex systems, giving one biblical example of each, and match the right engagement technique to each.
Identify how Scripture grounds interconnectedness and stewardship — seeing systems work as a form of caring for what belongs to God.
Interpret the Body of Christ (1 Corinthians 12) as a complex system whose health lies in the relationships among diverse parts, not the optimization of any one part.
Analyze a destructive social equilibrium (the Moloch trap) using multipolar-trap reasoning, and evaluate Josiah's reform as a change to the game's payoffs.
Trace how one of their own habits reflects a system they live inside, and redesign the system rather than resolving to try harder.
Practice epistemic humility (Proverbs 11:2; James 4:6) as the posture complexity demands and Scripture commands.

modules.title: 3. A Problem Well Stated
modules.description: from vague unease → to precisely naming the crisis generators, including the church's own attractional arms race.

steps.stepNarrative: from vague unease → to precisely naming the crisis generators, including the church's own attractional arms race.
learningObjectives: Define the metacrisis and name Schmachtenberger's three generators of existential risk.
Translate each generator into its church expression: attractional arms races, congregational externalities, and an eroded epistemic commons.
Interpret 1 Samuel 8 as the pattern of trading agency for god-like power, and evaluate where church and society repeat Israel's demand.
Articulate the biblical coupling of responsibility with power (Luke 12:48; Matthew 23:3-4; James 3:1) as the standard exponential capability must meet.
Propose one "third way" design principle for their own community — beyond authoritarian control and liberal chaos.

modules.title: 4. The Wisdom Gap & the Conditions for Trust
modules.description: from admiring wisdom → to building the trust conditions and practices that let wisdom scale.

steps.stepTitle: The Wisdom Gap & the Conditions for Trust
steps.stepNarrative: from admiring wisdom → to building the trust conditions and practices that let wisdom scale.
learningObjectives: Explain the Wisdom Gap and why wisdom, unlike information, only scales through relationships of trust.
Name the three conditions for the evolution of trust and locate each in the practices of a healthy congregation.
Analyze Jesus' "shrewd as snakes, innocent as doves" as the posture for building trust among wolves without becoming one.
Trace the traits by which righteous Old Testament leaders scaled wisdom — humility, obedience, justice, leading by example, renewal.
Complete the Mind the Gap exercise and identify one cause of the gap between their values and their current life.
Design one concrete change to their community's "game" that improves the conditions for trust.

steps.stepNarrative: Play it, don't just read about it: when does trust pay, and what makes it collapse?

The righteous leaders of the Old Testament form a composite blueprint: they sought God's wisdom above all else (Solomon, 1 Kings 3:5-14; Daniel 2:17-19); acted with humility (Moses, Numbers 12:3; David's repentance, 2 Samuel 12:13); priorit
Jesus' Kingdom wisdom.
